Title: Nanopause context-switch penalty — exploratory logs
Author: Liam O'Rourke
Purpose: Quick personal runbook and raw logs for measuring short-request context-switch overhead on multi-tenant GPU hosts. Goal: quantify per-request latency penalty when the runtime repeatedly preempts and restores KV cache / CUDA contexts for a mix of short (50–150 tokens) and long (800–2048 tokens) requests.
Summary / quick takeaways:
- Observed a consistent extra 6–18 ms p50 penalty per short request when preceded by a long request that caused an eviction of model context on A100 40GB host with two tenants.
- Penalty scales with cold KV cache size and quantization mode: FP16 had ~12–18ms extra, int8->int8-quantized path had ~6–9ms extra (likely because we pre-compile/int8 kernels and warm-up less heavy). 
- Batch size and request coalescing reduced penalty (single-request streams suffer most). Setting a short 5ms batching window eliminated ~60% of penalty in synthetic mix.
Env details (host / runtime):
- Host: n1-standard-like node with A100 40GB (Prod-sim cluster, isolated test pool)
- CUDA driver: 520.61
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit 5d3f7a2), with dynamic KV-cache eviction toggles enabled
- Model: llama-2-13b-instruct (fp16 / int8 variants)
- Quantization path: bitsandbytes int8-enabled multi-kernel
- Client harness: locust-derived harness (single-threaded client agents) + lightweight generator that alternates short/long
- Traffic pattern: Zipf-ish intermittent: 80% short, 20% long but long requests are bursty (clustered)
Test scenarios (each ran 3x, median repo:
A) Baseline: continuous short requests (50–80 tokens), warm cache
B) Long-only: continuous long requests (1024 tokens), warm cache
C) Alternating: 8 short -> 1 long repeated (emulates periodic large instructions)
D) Clustered long: 1 long every 30s with short stream otherwise
E) Batch window 5ms vs 20ms comparison on alternating pattern
Commands / harness notes:
- Worker: python harness/runner.py --pattern alternating --short 60 --long 1024 --qps 120 --clients 40
- Runtime flags: --kv-eviction-threshold=0.85 --context-persist=true --coalesce-window-ms=5/20
- Measurement: in-server tracing (token emit timestamps) + client-side end-to-end
Representative numbers (median of median:
- Scenario A (Baseline short-only, warm): p50=18, p95=34, p99=58, qps=850 sustained
- Scenario B (Long-only): p50=380, p95=610, p99=980, qps=22 (long CPU/GPU dominated)
- Scenario C (Alternating, coalesce-window=5ms): short requests (immediately following a long) p50=36 (+18 over A), p95=64, p99=112; short requests not following a long p50=20
- Scenario D (Clustered long, coalesce=5ms): short requests p50=30 (+12 over A), p95=58, p99=98
- Scenario E (Alternating, coalesce-window=20ms): short following long p50=24 (+6 over A), p95=46, p99=82
Interpretation / possible causes:
- Penalty is dominated by two factors: (1) KV cache miss / re-population cost (copying KV tensors back into GPU memory / warming the causal cache) and (2) CUDA context re-bind and possible kernel reinitialization if memory layout differs after an eviction.
- Int8 path shows smaller per-request penalty; hypothesis: int8 kernels have smaller workspace and faster restore times, plus lower memory pressure reduces eviction.
- Coalescing helps because it amortizes the restore across multiple short requests (one restore for the batch). Short coalesce window (5–20ms) is a practical knob.

Actionable experiments to run next (prio:
1) Repeat same alternating pattern but pin long requests to dedicated backplane (disable eviction by raising threshold to 0.99) and measure hit on qps/latency — if penalty disappears we confirm eviction is main culprit.
2) Run same experiments with coalesce-window adaptive: start 0ms, then 2ms,5ms,10ms,25ms to plot latency vs batching tradeoff curve (optimize for 99th percentile).
3) Measure memory allocation paths: instrument the runtime to log memcpy sizes and kernel reinit counts during restore.
4) Try compressed persistence (zstd) for KV snapshots — trade off CPU decompress vs GPU memcpy.
Notes / heuristics for production settin:
- For mixed workloads, prefer short coalesce windows (5–10ms) + conservative KV eviction thresholds (0.92-ish) to reduce p50 penalty without blowing GPU memory.
- Provide a routing policy where very long requests are sent to a separate tenancy pool (Dedicated) or have higher eviction grace.
- Offer a model variant with smaller context (trimmed history) for ultra-low-latency short-turn requests.
